title: Unpacking the MNET-CTC Collaboration Grants Call
summary: Maya and Daniel break down the newly published call for proposals under the Mekong Network to Counter Transnational Crime (MNET-CTC) programme, run by GI-TOC and the Australian Government. They explore the grant structure, target crime areas, community resilience focus, cross-border requirements, and key application timelines.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Welcome back. Today we are diving into a newly published call for proposals document issued by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, or GI-TOC, together with the Australian Government. The document details the MNET-CTC collaboration grants. That acronym stands for the Mekong Network to Counter Transnational Crime.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And for anyone tracking illicit economies, civil society interventions, or regional security across Southeast Asia, this is a really interesting document to look at. Grant calls often get treated as purely administrative paperwork, but when you look closely at the design, you see the strategic blueprint of how regional actors are trying to disrupt organized crime networks from the ground up.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. The target audience here really comprises non-governmental organizations, grassroots community groups, journalists, academics, and researchers who operate across the Mekong subregion. If you work on policy or follow how transnational syndicates impact local populations in Southeast Asia, this call sets out exactly where the funding, the network building, and the operational priorities are heading.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us start with the programme itself. What is MNET-CTC, and what is its core mandate as framed in the document?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: MNET-CTC is a multi-year programme implemented by GI-TOC in partnership with the Australian Government. The call notes that the programme is built on recognizing the transformative power of data and analysis. Its aim is to strengthen the evidence base on transnational organized crime trends, while raising awareness about the localized impacts of illicit markets across five countries in the Mekong subregion.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And those five countries are Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam. But there is a very deliberate nuance regarding Myanmar right in the document, isn't there?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, there is an explicit footnote. It specifies that engagement in Myanmar will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis, should the operating context allow. That reflects the precarious and volatile environment on the ground there, while still keeping the door open if feasible.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right. That makes complete sense given the ongoing conflict and governance breakdown in Myanmar. Now, looking at the substantive focus, what specific crime types does the call ask organizations to tackle?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The document specifies three organized crime types: illegal drugs, financial crime, and child sexual exploitation. And it emphasizes not just the crimes themselves, but also the drivers and enablers behind them. Projects must respond to and disrupt at least one of those three priority areas.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Those three areas cover a massive footprint across the Mekong basin. You have illicit narcotics production and trafficking, sophisticated financial fraud and money laundering schemes, and child sexual exploitation, which has increasingly taken on digital and cross-border dimensions in the region.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Indeed. But notice how GI-TOC and the Australian Government want applicants to approach them. The call repeatedly stresses a community approach and a resilience framework. In the text, resilience to organized crime at the community level is defined very clearly. It says there must be a clear link between criminality, its harmful impacts at the community level, and the specific levers that can be used to withstand, adapt to, and disrupt organized crime systems.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Withstand, adapt to, and disrupt. That phrasing is quite telling. It is acknowledging that law enforcement alone cannot simply arrest the problem away. Civil society groups, local community members, journalists, and researchers are often on the front lines, acting as the very first responders when organized crime establishes roots in a community.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That is almost word-for-word what the document highlights. It points out that civil society actors are frequently the first ones responding to the fallout of illicit markets. So the stated goal of the entire initiative is to ensure that key stakeholders from different levels of society across the Mekong subregion have the evidence, the capacity, and the relationships needed to inform and influence both policy and practice.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us dig into the collaboration aspect, because the word collaboration is right there in the title of the grant: MNET-CTC collaboration grants. How is that operationalized?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: This is central to the design. The call welcomes applications from organizations proposing innovative projects that involve collaboration among two or three organizations. And here is a crucial detail: collaborative proposals among organizations based in different countries across the Mekong will be prioritized.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Prioritizing cross-border partnerships. That directly mirrors the nature of the threat, doesn't it? Transnational criminal syndicates do not stop at the Mekong River or national borders. They exploit jurisdiction gaps between Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Myanmar, and Vietnam. So having civil society collaborate across those same national borders creates a counter-network.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. GI-TOC points out that the initiative is built on the approach that greater collaboration between people leads to more resilient community initiatives. When partners learn from one another, develop new skills, and connect their operational experiences across the region, their overall impact is reinforced. Now, the document does note that strong individual applications proposing other pathways toward collaboration will also be considered, but funding permitting. The clear preference is joint action.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What kinds of organizations are eligible to apply under this umbrella?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The target applicants list is quite diverse. It explicitly identifies community-based organizations, non-profit and non-governmental organizations, media organizations, women and youth organizations, and faith-based organizations. It also mentions that applications from other organizations may be considered under the broader grant guidelines.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: I find the explicit inclusion of media organizations, as well as women and youth groups and faith-based bodies, very compelling. In many Mekong communities, faith networks and youth movements have significant social capital, while independent investigative journalists uncover the mechanics of financial crime or illicit trade routes that official channels might overlook.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Absolutely. And for those applying jointly, the document lays down strict structural rules. In any joint application, the consortium must elect a single lead organization. That lead organization is responsible for submitting the application. All implementing partners must be clearly identified, and each partner must submit a formal letter of support.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: They also require clear internal governance, right? It mentions roles and responsibilities must be established, and partners must agree on the division of work and how grant funds will be transferred and allocated among them.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, precisely. That avoids ambiguity down the road. Now, let us talk about the funding scale and what is actually on the table. The call specifies that most grants will be between thirty thousand and sixty-five thousand Australian dollars. That is AUD 30,000 to AUD 65,000.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Thirty to sixty-five thousand Australian dollars. For a community-based organization or an investigative media outfit in the Mekong, that is a meaningful amount of targeted funding. What is the operational timeframe for these grants?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The implementation period will run for exactly one year: from February 15, 2027 to February 15, 2028. Elsewhere in the summary table it is summarized as February 2027 to February 2028.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the benefits go beyond just the monetary award. What else does a successful applicant receive?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The document lists several non-financial support mechanisms. First, there is direct capacity support for the organizations and their key partners. Second, grantees gain membership in the GI-TOC Resilience Fund Community and broader GI-TOC networks. That brings access to future learning, collaboration, and potential funding opportunities where relevant. And third, grantees get opportunities to participate in additional MNET-CTC workshops, development dialogues, and resilience dialogues on an ad hoc basis.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That is an important dimension. The Resilience Fund at GI-TOC is a well-established global platform that links local community actors facing organized crime across Latin America, Africa, and Asia. Plugging Mekong civil society into that global infrastructure means these local groups are not operating in isolation. They are backstopped by global expertise, research, and shared security practices.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. And it connects back to GI-TOC's role in the programme. The call explains that projects are designed and implemented by local civil society, but with the support and oversight of GI-TOC. That is intended to ensure that the activities remain responsive and adaptive to local community realities while drawing on collective and international best practices.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us walk through the application process and the timeline. If an organization wants to put in a bid, what do they actually have to do?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It is a two-step application process. Step one: applicants must complete a pre-application questionnaire. They must submit this questionnaire during the official opening solicitation period. Step two: only applicants that score highly on that pre-application questionnaire will be invited to submit a full proposal application and an activity-based budget.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That two-stage filter saves a lot of wasted effort for smaller organizations. You do not have to build out a line-item budget and a fifty-page narrative proposal upfront if your concept does not align with the core criteria.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. And when applicants do reach that second stage, the document advises them to carefully consider the length and complexity of their proposed activities when designing that activity-based budget request.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What about language accessibility? Often in international development and security funding, applications are restricted exclusively to English, which creates a huge barrier for frontline community groups in non-Anglophone regions.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: This call addresses that directly. Applications can be submitted in English or in one of the major Mekong languages: Khmer, Lao, Thai, or Vietnamese. Application documents in those languages are made available on the MNET-CTC Collaboration Grants webpage.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That is a significant point of inclusion. Allowing organizations to formulate their proposals in Khmer, Lao, Thai, or Vietnamese ensures that genuine grassroots groups, who might have the best community intelligence and deepest local trust, are not disqualified simply because of a language barrier.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Now, let us examine the timeline dates published in the document. The opening solicitation period runs from November 1, 2026 to December 7, 2026, closing at 23:59 Central European Time, or CET. The text explicitly notes that late applications will not be accepted.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And after December 7, 2026?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The assessment period is slated from December 8, 2026 through January 15, 2027. Then, successful applicants are expected to commence their grant activities in February 2027, with the official implementation period running through February 15, 2028.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: How do applicants submit the pre-application or reach out with inquiries?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The document provides an official email address: mnet-ctc-resilience@globalinitiative.net. Both inquiries and pre-applications must be sent to that address, and the pre-application must arrive before the deadline of December 7, 2026 at 23:59 CET. They also recommend that potential applicants read the full grant opportunity guidelines available on their website.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us take a step back and look at the broader strategic picture painted by this document. Why is an initiative like MNET-CTC focusing so heavily on civil society and community resilience in the Mekong right now?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: When you look at the Mekong subregion, transnational crime is deeply entrenched in illicit economies—from synthetic drug trafficking in the Golden Triangle to complex online scam compounds, financial fraud, and human trafficking, including child sexual exploitation. These syndicates often operate across border zones where state capacity may be fragmented or contested. The Australian Government and GI-TOC recognize that formal interstate enforcement alone has serious structural limitations.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And by investing in an evidence base built by local actors—NGOs, researchers, community monitors, journalists—you begin to create transparency around how these illicit markets actually operate. The MNET-CTC goal is very clear: equipping society with the evidence, capacity, and relationships to influence policy and practice. It is about creating sustainable accountability from within the region.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, building a community of practice. The text explicitly calls it a community of practice that collaboratively works to strengthen resilience. It links local actors, regional counterparts, government stakeholders, and even the private sector.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So, to wrap this up, what are the primary takeaways and what should our listeners keep an eye on?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: First, the scope: targeted civil society interventions addressing illegal drugs, financial crime, and child sexual exploitation across Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar—operating context permitting—Thailand, and Vietnam. Second, the mechanism: collaborative grants of AUD 30,000 to AUD 65,000, with a strong preference for multi-country Mekong partnerships. Third, the dual approach: direct community resilience paired with capacity building and membership in the GI-TOC Resilience Fund Community.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And for anyone looking to engage or track the process, keep the key window in mind: applications open November 1, 2026 and close December 7, 2026 at 23:59 CET, with implementation beginning in February 2027. It will be fascinating to see what kinds of cross-border alliances emerge from this call and how civil society in the Mekong continues to adapt to an evolving organized crime landscape.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: We will certainly be watching the outcomes and the research that emerges from these partnerships. Thank you for tuning in, and we will see you on the next deep-dive.
